title: The Marriage Is Still There… But When Did You Stop Choosing Each Other?
paragraphs: The Marriage Is Still There… But When Did You Stop Choosing Each Other?

You can remain faithful enough not to leave—and still become distant enough to make the person you married feel alone. Scripture points toward something better: a covenant where love does not merely stay, but keeps turning toward the beloved.
There is a kind of heartbreak nobody posts about.
No screaming match that wakes the neighbors.
Just two wedding rings still being worn by two people who slowly stopped reaching for each other.
They still ask who is picking up the groceries.
They still sleep in the same room.
They may even sit beside each other in church.
From the outside, everything looks intact.
But somewhere between deadlines, dishes, children, exhaustion, disappointments, ministry, financial pressure, unanswered texts, predictable routines, and conversations reduced to logistics…
And that is what makes this so dangerous.
Because marriages do not always collapse through one spectacular scandal.
Sometimes they simply become emotionally starved.
They just stopped expressing love with the intentionality they once considered natural.
Remember when hearing their voice changed your day?
Remember when you noticed tiny things?
Remember when you wanted to know what they were thinking?
Remember when a few hours apart felt long?
Remember when you dressed differently because you knew they would see you?
Remember when you prayed for God to let this person become your husband or wife?
Then somehow the person who once felt like an answered prayer became familiar enough to be taken for granted.
The person you once asked God for can eventually become the person you barely notice if gratitude is replaced by familiarity.
And perhaps one of the most sobering questions a married person can ask is not simply:
“Does my spouse still experience being loved by me?”
Those are not always the same question.

Scripture never presents biblical marriage as an endless romantic high. Marriage is covenant, and covenant survives seasons when emotion fluctuates. But covenant faithfulness should never become an excuse for emotional laziness.
The Bible's vision is deeper than merely remaining legally married.
It calls husband and wife toward sacrificial, embodied, attentive love.
The Greek word translated “love” is ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate, from agapaō.
Paul's command is striking because this love is not presented merely as something a husband happens to feel. It is something he is commanded to practice.
“...as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Jesus did not love His bride through passive sentiment.
Ultimately, His love went to a cross.
That does not mean a spouse becomes a savior. Only Jesus saves. It does mean Christian marriage is supposed to display something of Christ's self-giving love.
Instead of asking only, “What am I getting from this marriage?”
“How can I love this person in a way that reflects Jesus?”
It is putting down the phone because your spouse is trying to tell you something.
It is asking a second question instead of mechanically saying, “How was your day?”
It is remembering what has been weighing on them.
It is apologizing without adding, “but you…”
It is touching their hand when affection has become rare.
It is arranging time together instead of perpetually waiting for life to become less busy.
Saying thank you for things you have silently expected for years.
It is refusing to believe that because you already “won” their heart, you no longer need to care for it.
And Scripture gives us a surprisingly beautiful picture of marital delight.
The Song of Songs contains this line:
“I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine.”
The Hebrew word דּוֹדִי — dodi carries the sense of “my beloved.”
Not the person who takes out the trash.
Not the person who forgot the thing I reminded them about three times.
Marriage certainly contains responsibilities, but your spouse is more than the function they perform in your household.
They have fears they may not know how to articulate.
They have insecurities you may have forgotten.
A mind carrying pressures you may never completely see.
And perhaps they still want something they are embarrassed to ask you for:
To know that after all these years, you would still choose them.
Not merely because a certificate says you did once.
This is where some marriages quietly bleed.
One spouse thinks, “Of course I love you. I'm still here.”
The other thinks, “Then why don't I feel seen anymore?”
But physical proximity alone is not intimacy.
You can sleep twelve inches away from somebody whose heart feels twelve miles away.
And no, the answer is not manufacturing artificial romance.
It is not pretending every marriage should resemble a honeymoon.
It is not demanding expensive dates, luxury vacations, flowers every Friday, or cinematic gestures.
Some of the deepest pursuit costs almost nothing.
Sometimes five honest words can reach places a five-star dinner cannot.
But there is another side of this that needs to be said.
You cannot demand pursuit while refusing grace.
Marriage places two sinners close enough to discover that neither one is Jesus.
That discovery can either destroy unrealistic expectations or deepen dependence on Christ.
Christian marriage cannot survive indefinitely on chemistry alone because chemistry cannot forgive.
Date nights cannot regenerate the human heart.
Jesus must remain at the center.
Because eventually marriage exposes things dating could hide.
The need to always be right.
The tendency to punish with silence.
The habit of resurrecting forgiven failures whenever another argument begins.
And suddenly marriage becomes more than a love story.
Sometimes you look into that mirror and discover that the greatest threat to your marriage is not always what your spouse needs to change.
Sometimes God places His finger on you.
Your habit of giving strangers online more attention than the person sitting beside you.
But biblical conviction is not meant to leave us drowning in shame.
And repentance leads us toward Christ.
This is where our theme becomes more than a slogan:
Maybe your marriage already has a scandal.
Maybe trust has actually been shattered.
Maybe something happened that cannot be repaired by flowers and a romantic dinner.
Maybe years of resentment have accumulated.
Maybe emotional intimacy went somewhere it never belonged.
Maybe both of you are exhausted from repeating the same fight with different vocabulary.

Pursuing each other does not mean ignoring serious sin, concealing abuse, eliminating appropriate boundaries, or pretending trust can be instantly restored. Forgiveness, reconciliation, restored trust, accountability, safety, and consequences are related but distinct realities. Serious situations may require wise pastoral counsel and qualified professional help.
Grace is not pretending darkness is light.
Grace brings darkness into the light and asks Jesus to do what human pride cannot.
Because the Gospel begins with a truth every marriage desperately needs:
We are sinners who cannot rescue ourselves.
Yet God did not wait for humanity to make itself worthy before demonstrating His love.
“but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
That verse does not mean remaining passively in dangerous circumstances.
It means the Christian understanding of love begins with grace we did not earn.
And people who know they have been forgiven much should become people increasingly willing to repent, forgive, serve, and love.
That is why pursuing your spouse is ultimately bigger than romance.
Not because your spouse is worthy of worship.
But because honoring the covenant you made before God can glorify the God who taught you what covenant love means.
So maybe tonight you do not need another marriage article.
Maybe you need to walk across the room.
Look at the person you married.
Not at everything they have failed to become.
Remember the years that have happened to both of you.
“Have I made you feel pursued lately?”
Do not correct their memory halfway through their sentence.
Do not turn their pain into evidence against them.
Maybe their answer will encourage you.
Maybe you will discover they have been lonelier than you realized.
Maybe you will discover they thought you stopped caring because you were actually exhausted and did not know how to say it.
Maybe two people who have been silently waiting for the other person to move first will finally discover that pride has stolen enough time.
Why not the person reading this?
Not because your spouse deserves perfection.
Not because you can fix everything tonight.
But because Jesus has loved you too deeply for pride to have the final word.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness is needed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Rebuild slowly where rebuilding is needed.
Not the imaginary person you married years ago.
Pursue the person standing before you now.
The beautiful mystery of lifelong marriage is not merely getting to know somebody once.
It is being given decades to keep discovering who they are becoming.
Maybe that is part of what “growing old together” should mean.
Not merely aging beside each other.
Discovering each other again and again while both of you are being transformed by Christ.
But do more than date them.
And when life becomes brutally ordinary, refuse to confuse ordinary with worthless.
One day, if God gives you enough years together, you may look at hands covered in wrinkles that once slid a wedding ring onto yours.
You may wish you could return to one completely ordinary Tuesday.
Do not wait until something becomes a memory before recognizing that it was a gift.
And if this article exposed distance in your marriage, do not merely scroll into the next distraction.
Or send it privately and say, “Can we talk about this?”
Not to prove that your marriage is perfect.

But because another husband may need to wake up before emotional distance becomes a canyon. Another wife may need encouragement not to stop reaching. Another couple may be sitting beside each other tonight, each secretly wondering whether the other still cares.
If something here points people toward Christ, repentance, covenant faithfulness, forgiveness, and restoration, helping that truth travel farther can itself become an act offered for God's glory.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow.
But before you leave this page, look at your spouse again.
Maybe the greatest romantic gesture you make this year will not be a vacation.
Maybe it will be reaching across a distance neither of you knew how to cross and whispering:
“I don't want to merely stay married to you. By the grace of God, I want to keep learning how to love you.”
Because someday you may discover that the person you kept waiting to pursue was quietly waiting to be chosen by you again.
